# MPM Pumpkin Smash

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OVQAAlh-3s8)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates a multi-layered organic destruction setup where a pumpkin is smashed by an animated hammer in slow motion. The pumpkin is split into three distinct material layers -- outer skin, fibrous flesh, and seeds -- each with its own MPM material configuration. The tutorial covers the full production pipeline: material layering and point optimization, slow-motion time scaling with correct velocity handling, secondary debris emission, meshing with UV transfer and smoothing masks, and rendering the seed pieces using MPM Deform Pieces. This is one of the more involved example scenes, showcasing how to combine multiple material types and post-simulation nodes into a compact, production-ready setup.

## Key Concepts

### Multi-Layer Material Setup

The pumpkin is decomposed into three separate components, each modeled and configured independently:

- **Outer Skin** -- A thin shell with some thickness. Uses a material derived from the snow preset with compression hardening enabled. Provides the structural exterior that fractures on impact.
- **Flesh** -- Fibrous interior geometry with fibers oriented from the outer skin toward the core. This fiber orientation influences both the simulation behavior (how the material tears) and the render appearance. The material starts from the snow preset with zero compression hardening, then is iterated to achieve the desired look.
- **Seeds** -- Small seed models scattered and oriented toward the pumpkin center. These use a rubber-like preset and are simulated as rigid pieces that get deformed/moved by the MPM solver.

There is no single "correct" recipe for these materials. The approach is to start from a preset (snow or rubber), then iterate until the simulation produces the desired visual result.

### Point Optimization and Attribute Transfer

A key optimization technique is demonstrated: instead of using the points directly output by MPM Source, the flesh model's points are kept and fused to eliminate overlaps (reducing from 40 million to 9 million points). The MPM material attributes are then configured separately and transferred onto these optimized points. This proves that you do not need to simulate the exact points coming out of the MPM Source node -- you can configure materials on one set of points and transfer the attributes to another.

After merging all components (skin, flesh, seeds), another overlap-deletion pass reduces the total from 14 million to 12 million points. Finally, stiffness is globally increased across all materials based on simulation iteration.

### Slow-Motion Time Scaling

The simulation runs in slow motion using a time scale parameter on the MPM Solver. Several velocity adjustments are required to handle this correctly:

- **For rendering:** Velocity vectors must be multiplied by the time scale so they represent actual per-frame motion in the slowed-down timeline.
- **For debris emission:** Velocity vectors must be divided by the time scale to recover real-time velocities, because the secondary debris simulation needs proper physical velocities for correct behavior.
- The MPM Debris node automatically imports the time scale from the simulation branch, so features like "spread points along velocity" correctly account for slow motion without manual adjustment.

### Simulation Start Frame and Clamping

The simulation starts at frame 32 (when the hammer impact occurs). A "clamp to first frame" node ensures the pumpkin geometry is visible from frame 1 onward, even though no simulation runs until frame 32.

### Secondary Debris

The MPM Debris node generates source points for a secondary POP simulation. Configuration adjustments include:

- Increased minimum speed threshold to exclude slow-moving points from emission.
- Reduced point replication parameters to emit fewer particles.
- Only 10% of generated points are kept from the debris node output.
- Seeds are excluded from debris emission.

The secondary POP simulation includes air resistance (with packing-based attenuation so densely packed points resist drag more) and collision handling.

A separate secondary layer renders as tiny water droplets / spray for high-frequency detail. This layer also retains only 10% of points.

### Meshing with MPM Surface

The post-simulation meshing pipeline leverages MPM Surface and related nodes, which embed much of the previously manual technology into compact node trees.

**Skin Mesh:**
- A depth attribute is computed to vary the surface color between interior and exterior at render time (smooth transition between two colors).
- UVs are transferred from a rest model via the third input of MPM Surface.
- Surface parameters: no dilation, some smoothing, some erosion.
- Smoothing masks protect areas of interest: the JP attribute (tearing/stretching regions) and curvature-based masks both exclude high-detail areas from smoothing.

**Flesh Mesh:**
- Produces the fibrous look directly from the simulation.
- Adaptivity increased by a factor of 10 to reduce polygon count (target: fitting within GPU memory for Karma XPU). Even so, the mesh reaches approximately 28 million polygons.

**Seed Pieces:**
- Uses MPM Deform Pieces without the MPM Post Structure node.
- Each seed gets a name attribute, then MPM Deform Pieces moves the original seed models according to the simulated point motion.
- The deformed seeds retain UVs and other render attributes from the original models.
- Final output is baked to poly soup.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Generate simulation points from geometry | Particle separation (driven by MPM Container) |
| MPM Configure | Define material properties per layer | Preset: snow (skin/flesh), rubber (seeds); compression hardening: 0 (flesh), nonzero (skin); stiffness multiplied up globally |
| MPM Solver | Run the simulation | Material condition: 7; time scale (custom); domain wall deletion enabled |
| MPM Collider | Animated hammer collider | Default settings |
| MPM Surface | Mesh the simulated points | Dilation: off (skin); smoothing: on; erosion: on; mask smooth by JP attribute and curvature; adaptivity: 10x (flesh); VDB from particles mode |
| MPM Debris | Generate secondary particle sources | Minimum speed: increased; point replication: reduced; keep ratio: 10% |
| MPM Deform Pieces | Move seed models with sim data | Name attribute required on each piece |
| Clamp to First Frame | Show geometry before sim start | Sim starts at frame 32 |
| POP Solver | Secondary debris simulation | Air resistance with packing; collision handling |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Model the pumpkin layers** -- Split the pumpkin into skin (outer shell with thickness), flesh (fibrous interior oriented toward core), and seeds (small models scattered and oriented toward center).
2. **Optimize point counts** -- Keep geometry points, fuse overlapping points to reduce count significantly, then configure MPM materials separately and transfer attributes.
3. **Configure materials** -- Start from presets (snow for skin/flesh, rubber for seeds). Iterate on compression hardening, stiffness, and other parameters until the simulation looks right. Increase global stiffness as needed.
4. **Set up the collider** -- Animate the hammer in real time at the expected impact speed. Apply the simulation time scale to achieve slow motion.
5. **Configure the MPM Solver** -- Set material condition to 7 for more aggressive substepping. Enable domain wall deletion for escaping points. Set the time scale parameter.
6. **Handle simulation start frame** -- Use a clamp-to-first-frame node so the pumpkin is visible before the impact frame (frame 32).
7. **Adjust velocity for rendering** -- Multiply velocity vectors by the time scale so motion blur renders correctly in the slow-motion timeline.
8. **Generate debris sources** -- Use MPM Debris with increased minimum speed, reduced point replication, and 10% retention. Exclude seeds. Reverse the velocity time-scale adjustment so debris emits with real-time velocities.
9. **Simulate secondaries** -- Run a POP simulation with air resistance (packing-aware) and collisions. Add a second spray/droplet layer for high-frequency detail, also at 10% retention.
10. **Mesh the skin** -- Use MPM Surface with smoothing and erosion. Transfer UVs from rest model via third input. Compute depth attribute for render-time color variation. Enable smoothing masks on JP (tearing) and curvature to protect detail.
11. **Mesh the flesh** -- Use MPM Surface with VDB from particles and 10x adaptivity to manage polygon count for GPU rendering.
12. **Deform the seeds** -- Assign name attributes to seeds, then use MPM Deform Pieces to move the original high-quality seed models. Bake to poly soup.

## Tips & Insights

- You do not need to use the points output by MPM Source directly. You can configure materials on a separate point set and transfer the attributes, which allows point-count optimization via fusing.
- Start from material presets and iterate. There is no single correct recipe for organic destruction -- tweak compression hardening, stiffness, and other parameters until you achieve the desired look.
- When working in slow motion, remember that velocity vectors need different scaling depending on context: multiply by time scale for rendering (motion blur), divide by time scale for secondary emission (physical accuracy).
- The MPM Debris node automatically imports time scale from the simulation, so "spread points along velocity" works correctly without manual adjustment.
- Use smoothing masks (JP attribute and curvature) on MPM Surface to protect high-detail areas like tears and sharp features from being smoothed away.
- Increase MPM Surface adaptivity to reduce polygon count when targeting GPU renderers like Karma XPU.
- For rigid pieces within an MPM simulation (like seeds), use MPM Deform Pieces to drive high-quality source models rather than meshing the simulated points directly.
- The post-simulation node tree in Houdini 21 is much more compact than in previous versions, with most meshing technology embedded directly in the MPM Surface and related nodes.

# MPM Car Rain

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mKg7OWiBQE4)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video walks through a rain-on-car scene that uses MPM to simulate water splashes on a vehicle surface, with water trickling down the bodywork and collecting on geometric lips before overflowing. The setup is notable for combining procedural raindrop impact modeling, a reverse-time rain animation trick for synchronized splashes, surface tension-driven water behavior, and a rendering fix for total internal reflection artifacts. Additional non-MPM layers include condensation droplets that respond to flowing water and a dynamic puddle with ripple simulation. This is an excellent example of a production-quality environmental FX shot built around a relatively simple MPM simulation.

## Key Concepts

### Car Model Preparation

The car model is prepared in multiple versions for different purposes:

- **Render version** -- Windows are given thickness to produce proper refraction in the renderer.
- **Watertight collider version** -- A simplified, watertight mesh generated for collision detection in the MPM simulation.

### Procedural Raindrop Impact Modeling

Rather than simulating falling raindrops with MPM (which would be wasteful), only the splash impacts are simulated. The impact locations and splash shapes are built procedurally:

1. A grid is placed above the car and points are scattered on it.
2. Points are projected down onto the car surface to define impact locations.
3. A coordinate frame is constructed at each impact point using the surface normal as the up vector, with random normal variation for rotational diversity.
4. A circle/ring is copied to each impact point, representing the splash footprint.
5. The splash shape (a crown pattern) is modeled procedurally, then converted via VDB from Particles.
6. Velocity is transferred back to the splash mesh for use as the MPM source.

### Reverse-Time Rain Synchronization

A clever technique synchronizes falling raindrops with their splash impacts:

1. Start from each raindrop's known impact position on the car.
2. Reverse time from the end of the simulation (frame 160, with padding) backward.
3. Simulate the raindrops lifting away from the car back to their emission origins.
4. Delete each raindrop when it reaches its starting height.
5. Flip time and velocity again to produce a forward-playing rain animation.

The result is rain that is perfectly synchronized with the MPM splash emission -- when each raindrop hits the car, the corresponding splash crown is ready to be sourced into the MPM simulation. The raindrops themselves are rendered as instanced spheres and are never simulated with MPM.

### Surface Tension and Water Behavior

The MPM simulation uses the water preset with strong surface tension. This drives the realistic behavior of water collecting on geometric edges and lips of the car body:

- Water trickles down the car surface.
- It gathers at geometric lips and edges.
- When enough water accumulates, it overflows and pours to the next level downstream.

This behavior matches real-world expectations of water running over complex automotive surfaces.

### Collision Settings for Thin Geometry

Two collision adjustments are critical for this scene:

- **Particle-level collision** is enabled to achieve precise interaction with thin car body panels.
- **Collision detection distance** is increased above the default of 1. Without this, particles struggle to stick to the underside of geometry. Increasing the detection distance allows water to convincingly adhere to overhanging surfaces and collect at lips.

### Index of Refraction Fix for Thin Water Sheets

A rendering artifact occurs when thin water sheets sit on the car surface: small air gaps between the water and the metal cause total internal reflection. Light rays entering the water hit the water-air interface at a shallow angle and reflect back inside the water instead of passing through to the car surface. This causes unrealistic bright reflections where the water samples the HDR environment instead of the car paint beneath.

The fix uses a distance-based IOR attribute:

- Compute the distance from each mesh point to the car collider surface.
- Points very close to the car (purple in visualization) get IOR set to 1.0 (no refraction -- light passes straight through).
- Points farther from the car (red in visualization) keep the normal water IOR of 1.33.
- In the shader, the IOR attribute is remapped from 0-1 to 0-1.33 and fed into the refraction input.

### Mist Burst Layer

A separate branch models mist bursts at each raindrop impact location. These are small, fast-moving particles simulated with a POP solver (not MPM), rendered as very small droplets to add high-frequency detail to the splash impacts.

### Condensation Layer

A non-MPM detail layer simulates condensation droplets on the car surface:

1. Many small points are scattered across the car surface with assigned pscale values.
2. A solver tracks whether MPM water is flowing over each condensation point.
3. When water flows over a point, its pscale is reduced to near zero (condensation is "wiped away").
4. Over time without water flow, the pscale gradually restores (condensation reforms).
5. A condensation attribute controls the effect, visualized as red (full pscale) to purple (reduced).

### Dynamic Puddle with Ripple Simulation

Water particles that exit the simulation domain in front of the car drive a dynamic puddle effect:

1. A grid section is extracted in front of the car.
2. Points about to be deleted at the domain boundary are projected onto the puddle grid.
3. These points displace the grid surface.
4. A ripple solver creates wave propagation from the displacement points.
5. The final amplitude is scaled to 25% to keep the effect subtle.

Static puddles are also placed around the car for environmental context.

### Meshing the MPM Simulation

The MPM Surface node uses VDB from Particles with sequential filtering: dilation, erosion, then smoothing. This sequence produces a reasonable liquid look. The Neural Point Surface with liquid model is mentioned as a potential alternative but was not used in this scene.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Source the splash crown meshes | Continuous emission enabled |
| MPM Configure | Water material setup | Preset: water (default settings) |
| MPM Solver | Simulate water splashes | Surface tension: strong; min substeps: increased; material condition: reduced; substeps doubled |
| MPM Collider | Car body collision | Particle-level collision: enabled; detection distance: increased above default of 1 |
| MPM Surface | Mesh the water simulation | VDB from Particles; dilation, erosion, smoothing applied in sequence |
| VDB from Particles | Build splash crown shapes | Used in splash modeling branch |
| POP Solver | Mist burst simulation | Separate from MPM, renders as tiny droplets |
| Ripple Solver | Dynamic puddle waves | Amplitude scaled to 25% |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Prepare the car model** -- Add thickness to windows for refraction. Generate a watertight version for collision.
2. **Define raindrop impact locations** -- Scatter points on a grid above the car, project onto the car surface. Build oriented frames using surface normals with random rotation.
3. **Model the splash crowns** -- Copy a circle to each impact point. Procedurally shape the splash crown geometry. Convert to VDB, transfer velocity back to the mesh for MPM sourcing.
4. **Create synchronized rain** -- Use the reverse-time technique: start from impact positions, simulate backward to emission origins, then flip time and velocity. Instance spheres on the raindrop points for rendering.
5. **Configure the MPM simulation** -- Use the water preset with strong surface tension. Increase minimum substeps for stability. Reduce material condition. Double substeps. Enable particle-level collision and increase detection distance.
6. **Kill exiting particles** -- Delete points that hit the ground to conserve memory.
7. **Build the mist layer** -- Model mist burst shapes at impact locations. Simulate with a POP solver for fast, small particles.
8. **Mesh the water** -- Use MPM Surface with VDB from Particles. Apply dilation, erosion, and smoothing in sequence.
9. **Fix IOR for thin water sheets** -- Compute distance to car surface. Set IOR to 1.0 for points close to the car, 1.33 for points farther away. Remap in the shader from 0-1 to 0-1.33.
10. **Add condensation** -- Scatter points on car. Use a solver to reduce pscale when MPM water flows over them and restore pscale over time.
11. **Create the ground and puddles** -- Build a ground plane with static puddles. Add a dynamic puddle in front of the car driven by deleted simulation particles, with a ripple solver at 25% amplitude.

## Tips & Insights

- Simulate only the splashes with MPM, not the falling raindrops. Instance spheres on the rain points and render them separately to save significant memory.
- The reverse-time rain trick ensures perfect synchronization between raindrop impacts and splash emission without complex timing logic.
- Increase collision detection distance above the default of 1 when you need water to stick to the underside of geometry or collect at surface lips. This is essential for realistic water behavior on complex surfaces.
- Enable particle-level collision for precise interaction with thin geometry like car body panels.
- Watch for total internal reflection artifacts when rendering thin water sheets on surfaces. Use a distance-based IOR attribute (1.0 near the surface, 1.33 farther away) to eliminate the problem in the shader.
- Strong surface tension requires more substeps for stability. Increase minimum substeps and reduce the material condition number to compensate.
- Kill particles at domain boundaries to manage memory, especially in scenes with continuous emission.
- The dynamic puddle recommendation: extend it along the sides of the car (not just the front) for better integration of water being deleted at domain edges.
- The Neural Point Surface with liquid model is a viable alternative to VDB from Particles for meshing water simulations.

# MPM Wolf Snow

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JUcON39F7zE)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates a character-interaction snow simulation where three wolves run through a snow-covered terrain, kicking up particles and leaving trails. The setup showcases several advanced optimization techniques: camera frustum culling to limit the simulation domain, depth-based volume tapering to reduce point counts beneath the surface, and the MPM sleeping mechanism to deactivate passive particles. The tutorial also covers terrain preparation, static/dynamic snow splitting, secondary debris emission, volume rendering with SDF masking to preserve snow structure, and environmental dressing with snow-covered trees.

## Key Concepts

### Wolf Asset Preparation

The wolf animation (sourced from the SideFX content library) is prepared through several stages:

- **Animation smoothing** -- The raw animation is smoothed before further processing.
- **Fur simulation** -- A Vellum simulation is run on the wolf's fur guides, then cached.
- **Duplication** -- The single wolf is duplicated to create three wolves running through the scene.
- **Multiple output versions** -- The wolf geometry is prepared in different forms: a collider version (body + fur rasterized as VDB), a render version (with computed velocity for motion blur), and the fur itself for final Karma rendering.

### Camera Frustum Culling for Simulation Domain

A significant optimization technique clips the simulation domain to only what the camera sees:

1. Trail the wolves' paths over the first ~100 frames to establish their trajectories.
2. Compare the trajectories against the render camera's frustum.
3. Clip the snow volume to only the region visible to the camera (with padding before and after the visible range).
4. Convert the clipped region to VDB for use as the simulation domain boundary.

This avoids simulating snow in areas that will never appear on screen.

### Terrain and Snow Volume Construction

The snow terrain is built procedurally:

1. Generate a bounding box around the wolf trajectories.
2. Set the snow thickness.
3. Add surface detail (noise patterns simulating wind-sculpted snow patches).
4. Convert to SDF.
5. Cut out the camera-visible simulation region.

### Depth-Based Volume Tapering

An optimization reduces the simulated volume beneath the snow surface:

1. Observe how deep the wolf paws penetrate the snow.
2. Project the snow volume's bottom surface toward the wolves.
3. At greater depth, pull the volume boundary closer to where the paws actually reach.
4. Near the surface, lerp back to the original snow volume boundary.

This reduces the total simulation volume while keeping sufficient depth where the wolves interact with the snow, allowing higher resolution where it matters.

### Static vs. Dynamic Snow Splitting

The snow is split into two categories:

- **Dynamic snow** -- The region around the wolf paths, filled with MPM points that will be actively simulated. This is the carved-out region after frustum culling and depth tapering.
- **Static snow** -- Everything else visible to the camera, rendered as a static collider. A hole is cut in the static snow where the dynamic region exists.

To ensure seamless blending at render time, fine surface detail (bumpiness) is added to the static snow mesh to match the granular texture that MPM points produce when rasterized to a density grid.

An extension mesh covers any remaining areas visible to the camera that neither the dynamic nor the initial static snow covers.

### Collider Configuration

Two collider types are used with different friction/stickiness settings:

- **Wolf collider (deforming)** -- Body + rasterized fur VDB. Low stickiness so snow does not adhere excessively to the paws.
- **Static snow collider** -- High stickiness, simulating wet snow bonding to other wet snow, as expected in nature.

### Snow Material and Stiffness Noise

The dynamic snow uses the snow preset with modifications:

- Stiffness is multiplied up slightly to produce larger cohesive chunks.
- Noise is applied to stiffness values to add variation. The noise is remapped to a range of 5 to 2, then multiplied against the base stiffness. Any noise pattern works; the key is introducing spatial variation.

### Sleeping Mechanism for Performance

The sleeping (deactivation) system is critical for this mostly-passive simulation:

- The velocity threshold for deactivation is increased to make the solver more aggressive about putting particles to sleep.
- Particles far from the wolves' influence quickly become passive, saving significant computation.
- The simulation state can be visualized: purple = passive/sleeping, pink = active, with boundary particles also visible.
- A detail attribute string provides real-time statistics (e.g., "50% active, 44% passive, 5% boundary"). This can be linked to a Font SOP for on-screen stats during flipbooks.
- By the end of the simulation, up to 98% of particles may be passive at any given frame.

### Meshing Snow to SDF

The simulated MPM snow is converted to an SDF using VDB from Particles with conservative filtering:

- Dilation and erosion are kept small to preserve the granular look rather than creating sticky-looking clumps.
- Smoothing is applied to create a distribution of detail frequencies: smooth patches, mid-frequency shapes, and high-frequency small bits of snow.
- The goal is a natural mix of low, mid, and high frequency surface detail.

### Volume Rendering with SDF Masking

For rendering snow as a density volume, the "mask by surface" toggle on MPM Surface is essential:

- Without masking: The rasterized density looks uniformly fuzzy and grainy, lacking structural definition.
- With masking: The SDF representation is used as a mask on the density grid, preserving the overall snow structure while retaining fine particle detail.

This produces volumes with clear structural shapes plus granular surface texture, which is the desired look for snow.

### Secondary Debris

The MPM Debris node generates source points for a secondary POP simulation:

- JP attribute (stretching) multiplier increased to 5x to reduce emission from stretched areas.
- Slow-moving particle emission multiplier increased to 2x to reduce that source as well.
- Point replication reduced from 5 to 3 in both dimensions.
- Everything else at default.

The secondary simulation uses the same POP network pattern as other shots in the series. The debris is also rasterized to a density grid using MPM Surface, with the voxel size matched to the main simulation. The density multiplier for the secondary particles is typically dialed in during rendering in LOPs/Karma rather than in SOPs.

### Environmental Dressing

Trees are instanced on both sides of the wolf paths with snow added to branches. This is optional environmental detail handled in the LOP network and TOP network. The TOP network has significant baking requirements for the tree snow, which can be skipped if not needed.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Fill the dynamic snow volume with points | Snow preset |
| MPM Configure | Set snow material properties | Preset: snow; stiffness: multiplied up; stiffness noise: remapped 5-2 range |
| MPM Solver | Simulate snow interaction | Sleeping: enabled; velocity threshold: increased for aggressive deactivation |
| MPM Collider (wolves) | Deforming wolf body + fur collider | Low stickiness/friction |
| MPM Collider (static snow) | Static terrain collider | High stickiness (wet snow behavior) |
| MPM Surface | Mesh/rasterize snow points | VDB from Particles; small dilation/erosion; mask by surface: enabled |
| MPM Debris | Generate secondary particle sources | JP multiplier: 5x; slow particle multiplier: 2x; point replication: 3 (both axes) |
| Vellum Solver | Fur simulation on wolf guides | Pre-cached |
| Trail SOP | Track wolf trajectories | ~100 frames baked |
| VDB from Particles | Convert terrain to SDF | Used in terrain construction |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Prepare the wolf asset** -- Smooth the animation. Run a Vellum fur simulation and cache it. Duplicate the wolf to create three instances. Generate collider, render, and fur versions.
2. **Trail the wolf paths** -- Compute trajectories over the first ~100 frames to understand where the wolves travel through the scene.
3. **Clip to camera frustum** -- Use the render camera to identify the visible region. Clip the wolf paths and snow volume to this region with padding. Convert to VDB.
4. **Build the terrain** -- Generate a bounding box around the wolves. Set snow thickness and add wind-sculpted surface detail noise. Convert to SDF.
5. **Taper the volume by depth** -- Project the bottom surface toward the wolves at depth, lerp back to original near the surface. This reduces simulation volume while maintaining depth where paws interact.
6. **Split static and dynamic snow** -- The carved region becomes dynamic MPM snow. Everything else becomes a static collider with a hole cut for the dynamic region. Add surface bumpiness to the static mesh for blending.
7. **Add camera-fill extensions** -- Create additional static snow geometry to cover any remaining camera-visible areas.
8. **Configure colliders** -- Set wolves to deforming collider with low stickiness. Set static snow to high stickiness for wet-snow behavior.
9. **Configure the snow material** -- Use the snow preset. Multiply stiffness slightly. Apply noise (remapped 5-2) to stiffness for spatial variation.
10. **Enable sleeping** -- Activate the sleeping mechanism with an increased velocity threshold for aggressive deactivation of passive particles.
11. **Simulate** -- Run the MPM simulation. Monitor the state attribute for active/passive/boundary particle ratios.
12. **Mesh the snow** -- Convert to SDF using VDB from Particles with small dilation/erosion. Enable "mask by surface" for volume rendering to preserve snow structure.
13. **Generate and simulate debris** -- Use MPM Debris with increased JP and slow-particle multipliers, reduced point replication. Run through the standard POP debris network.
14. **Rasterize debris to density** -- Use MPM Surface matching the main simulation voxel size. Merge with the main snow volume. Adjust density multiplier at render time in LOPs.
15. **Dress the environment** -- Optionally instance snow-covered trees along the wolf paths via LOP and TOP networks.

## Tips & Insights

- Camera frustum culling is one of the most impactful optimizations for character-interaction snow scenes. Only simulate what the camera actually sees.
- Depth-based volume tapering further reduces simulation cost by narrowing the snow volume at depth where the wolves' paws do not reach, while keeping full volume near the surface.
- The sleeping mechanism can reduce active particle counts to as low as 2% of total particles in mostly-passive scenes. Increase the velocity threshold to make deactivation more aggressive.
- The detail attribute string on the simulation output provides real-time active/passive/boundary particle statistics. Link it to a Font SOP for visual monitoring during flipbooks.
- When meshing snow, keep dilation and erosion small to preserve the granular look. The goal is a natural mix of low, mid, and high frequency surface detail.
- Always enable "mask by surface" when rendering snow as density volumes. Without it, the rasterized density looks uniformly fuzzy and loses structural definition.
- Match static snow surface detail to the granularity of the rasterized dynamic snow points to ensure seamless blending at render time.
- Stiffness noise (any noise pattern, remapped to a useful range and multiplied against base stiffness) adds natural variation to how snow chunks break apart.
- For static colliders representing existing snow, use high stickiness to simulate wet snow bonding. For character colliders, use low stickiness so snow does not excessively adhere.
- Particles exiting the camera frustum can be killed to further optimize the simulation -- this is left as an exercise but is straightforward to implement.
- Density multiplier for secondary debris is best adjusted during rendering in LOPs/Karma, not in the SOP-level setup.

# MPM Pumpkin Smash

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OVQAAlh-3s8)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates a multi-layered organic destruction setup where a pumpkin is smashed by an animated hammer in slow motion. The pumpkin is split into three distinct material layers -- outer skin, fibrous flesh, and seeds -- each with its own MPM material configuration. The tutorial covers the full production pipeline: material layering and point optimization, slow-motion time scaling with correct velocity handling, secondary debris emission, meshing with UV transfer and smoothing masks, and rendering the seed pieces using MPM Deform Pieces. This is one of the more involved example scenes, showcasing how to combine multiple material types and post-simulation nodes into a compact, production-ready setup.

## Key Concepts

### Multi-Layer Material Setup

The pumpkin is decomposed into three separate components, each modeled and configured independently:

- **Outer Skin** -- A thin shell with some thickness. Uses a material derived from the snow preset with compression hardening enabled. Provides the structural exterior that fractures on impact.
- **Flesh** -- Fibrous interior geometry with fibers oriented from the outer skin toward the core. This fiber orientation influences both the simulation behavior (how the material tears) and the render appearance. The material starts from the snow preset with zero compression hardening, then is iterated to achieve the desired look.
- **Seeds** -- Small seed models scattered and oriented toward the pumpkin center. These use a rubber-like preset and are simulated as rigid pieces that get deformed/moved by the MPM solver.

There is no single "correct" recipe for these materials. The approach is to start from a preset (snow or rubber), then iterate until the simulation produces the desired visual result.

### Point Optimization and Attribute Transfer

A key optimization technique is demonstrated: instead of using the points directly output by MPM Source, the flesh model's points are kept and fused to eliminate overlaps (reducing from 40 million to 9 million points). The MPM material attributes are then configured separately and transferred onto these optimized points. This proves that you do not need to simulate the exact points coming out of the MPM Source node -- you can configure materials on one set of points and transfer the attributes to another.

After merging all components (skin, flesh, seeds), another overlap-deletion pass reduces the total from 14 million to 12 million points. Finally, stiffness is globally increased across all materials based on simulation iteration.

### Slow-Motion Time Scaling

The simulation runs in slow motion using a time scale parameter on the MPM Solver. Several velocity adjustments are required to handle this correctly:

- **For rendering:** Velocity vectors must be multiplied by the time scale so they represent actual per-frame motion in the slowed-down timeline.
- **For debris emission:** Velocity vectors must be divided by the time scale to recover real-time velocities, because the secondary debris simulation needs proper physical velocities for correct behavior.
- The MPM Debris node automatically imports the time scale from the simulation branch, so features like "spread points along velocity" correctly account for slow motion without manual adjustment.

### Simulation Start Frame and Clamping

The simulation starts at frame 32 (when the hammer impact occurs). A "clamp to first frame" node ensures the pumpkin geometry is visible from frame 1 onward, even though no simulation runs until frame 32.

### Secondary Debris

The MPM Debris node generates source points for a secondary POP simulation. Configuration adjustments include:

- Increased minimum speed threshold to exclude slow-moving points from emission.
- Reduced point replication parameters to emit fewer particles.
- Only 10% of generated points are kept from the debris node output.
- Seeds are excluded from debris emission.

The secondary POP simulation includes air resistance (with packing-based attenuation so densely packed points resist drag more) and collision handling.

A separate secondary layer renders as tiny water droplets / spray for high-frequency detail. This layer also retains only 10% of points.

### Meshing with MPM Surface

The post-simulation meshing pipeline leverages MPM Surface and related nodes, which embed much of the previously manual technology into compact node trees.

**Skin Mesh:**
- A depth attribute is computed to vary the surface color between interior and exterior at render time (smooth transition between two colors).
- UVs are transferred from a rest model via the third input of MPM Surface.
- Surface parameters: no dilation, some smoothing, some erosion.
- Smoothing masks protect areas of interest: the JP attribute (tearing/stretching regions) and curvature-based masks both exclude high-detail areas from smoothing.

**Flesh Mesh:**
- Produces the fibrous look directly from the simulation.
- Adaptivity increased by a factor of 10 to reduce polygon count (target: fitting within GPU memory for Karma XPU). Even so, the mesh reaches approximately 28 million polygons.

**Seed Pieces:**
- Uses MPM Deform Pieces without the MPM Post Structure node.
- Each seed gets a name attribute, then MPM Deform Pieces moves the original seed models according to the simulated point motion.
- The deformed seeds retain UVs and other render attributes from the original models.
- Final output is baked to poly soup.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Generate simulation points from geometry | Particle separation (driven by MPM Container) |
| MPM Configure | Define material properties per layer | Preset: snow (skin/flesh), rubber (seeds); compression hardening: 0 (flesh), nonzero (skin); stiffness multiplied up globally |
| MPM Solver | Run the simulation | Material condition: 7; time scale (custom); domain wall deletion enabled |
| MPM Collider | Animated hammer collider | Default settings |
| MPM Surface | Mesh the simulated points | Dilation: off (skin); smoothing: on; erosion: on; mask smooth by JP attribute and curvature; adaptivity: 10x (flesh); VDB from particles mode |
| MPM Debris | Generate secondary particle sources | Minimum speed: increased; point replication: reduced; keep ratio: 10% |
| MPM Deform Pieces | Move seed models with sim data | Name attribute required on each piece |
| Clamp to First Frame | Show geometry before sim start | Sim starts at frame 32 |
| POP Solver | Secondary debris simulation | Air resistance with packing; collision handling |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Model the pumpkin layers** -- Split the pumpkin into skin (outer shell with thickness), flesh (fibrous interior oriented toward core), and seeds (small models scattered and oriented toward center).
2. **Optimize point counts** -- Keep geometry points, fuse overlapping points to reduce count significantly, then configure MPM materials separately and transfer attributes.
3. **Configure materials** -- Start from presets (snow for skin/flesh, rubber for seeds). Iterate on compression hardening, stiffness, and other parameters until the simulation looks right. Increase global stiffness as needed.
4. **Set up the collider** -- Animate the hammer in real time at the expected impact speed. Apply the simulation time scale to achieve slow motion.
5. **Configure the MPM Solver** -- Set material condition to 7 for more aggressive substepping. Enable domain wall deletion for escaping points. Set the time scale parameter.
6. **Handle simulation start frame** -- Use a clamp-to-first-frame node so the pumpkin is visible before the impact frame (frame 32).
7. **Adjust velocity for rendering** -- Multiply velocity vectors by the time scale so motion blur renders correctly in the slow-motion timeline.
8. **Generate debris sources** -- Use MPM Debris with increased minimum speed, reduced point replication, and 10% retention. Exclude seeds. Reverse the velocity time-scale adjustment so debris emits with real-time velocities.
9. **Simulate secondaries** -- Run a POP simulation with air resistance (packing-aware) and collisions. Add a second spray/droplet layer for high-frequency detail, also at 10% retention.
10. **Mesh the skin** -- Use MPM Surface with smoothing and erosion. Transfer UVs from rest model via third input. Compute depth attribute for render-time color variation. Enable smoothing masks on JP (tearing) and curvature to protect detail.
11. **Mesh the flesh** -- Use MPM Surface with VDB from Particles and 10x adaptivity to manage polygon count for GPU rendering.
12. **Deform the seeds** -- Assign name attributes to seeds, then use MPM Deform Pieces to move the original high-quality seed models. Bake to poly soup.

## Tips & Insights

- You do not need to use the points output by MPM Source directly. You can configure materials on a separate point set and transfer the attributes, which allows point-count optimization via fusing.
- Start from material presets and iterate. There is no single correct recipe for organic destruction -- tweak compression hardening, stiffness, and other parameters until you achieve the desired look.
- When working in slow motion, remember that velocity vectors need different scaling depending on context: multiply by time scale for rendering (motion blur), divide by time scale for secondary emission (physical accuracy).
- The MPM Debris node automatically imports time scale from the simulation, so "spread points along velocity" works correctly without manual adjustment.
- Use smoothing masks (JP attribute and curvature) on MPM Surface to protect high-detail areas like tears and sharp features from being smoothed away.
- Increase MPM Surface adaptivity to reduce polygon count when targeting GPU renderers like Karma XPU.
- For rigid pieces within an MPM simulation (like seeds), use MPM Deform Pieces to drive high-quality source models rather than meshing the simulated points directly.
- The post-simulation node tree in Houdini 21 is much more compact than in previous versions, with most meshing technology embedded directly in the MPM Surface and related nodes.

# MPM Car Rain

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mKg7OWiBQE4)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video walks through a rain-on-car scene that uses MPM to simulate water splashes on a vehicle surface, with water trickling down the bodywork and collecting on geometric lips before overflowing. The setup is notable for combining procedural raindrop impact modeling, a reverse-time rain animation trick for synchronized splashes, surface tension-driven water behavior, and a rendering fix for total internal reflection artifacts. Additional non-MPM layers include condensation droplets that respond to flowing water and a dynamic puddle with ripple simulation. This is an excellent example of a production-quality environmental FX shot built around a relatively simple MPM simulation.

## Key Concepts

### Car Model Preparation

The car model is prepared in multiple versions for different purposes:

- **Render version** -- Windows are given thickness to produce proper refraction in the renderer.
- **Watertight collider version** -- A simplified, watertight mesh generated for collision detection in the MPM simulation.

### Procedural Raindrop Impact Modeling

Rather than simulating falling raindrops with MPM (which would be wasteful), only the splash impacts are simulated. The impact locations and splash shapes are built procedurally:

1. A grid is placed above the car and points are scattered on it.
2. Points are projected down onto the car surface to define impact locations.
3. A coordinate frame is constructed at each impact point using the surface normal as the up vector, with random normal variation for rotational diversity.
4. A circle/ring is copied to each impact point, representing the splash footprint.
5. The splash shape (a crown pattern) is modeled procedurally, then converted via VDB from Particles.
6. Velocity is transferred back to the splash mesh for use as the MPM source.

### Reverse-Time Rain Synchronization

A clever technique synchronizes falling raindrops with their splash impacts:

1. Start from each raindrop's known impact position on the car.
2. Reverse time from the end of the simulation (frame 160, with padding) backward.
3. Simulate the raindrops lifting away from the car back to their emission origins.
4. Delete each raindrop when it reaches its starting height.
5. Flip time and velocity again to produce a forward-playing rain animation.

The result is rain that is perfectly synchronized with the MPM splash emission -- when each raindrop hits the car, the corresponding splash crown is ready to be sourced into the MPM simulation. The raindrops themselves are rendered as instanced spheres and are never simulated with MPM.

### Surface Tension and Water Behavior

The MPM simulation uses the water preset with strong surface tension. This drives the realistic behavior of water collecting on geometric edges and lips of the car body:

- Water trickles down the car surface.
- It gathers at geometric lips and edges.
- When enough water accumulates, it overflows and pours to the next level downstream.

This behavior matches real-world expectations of water running over complex automotive surfaces.

### Collision Settings for Thin Geometry

Two collision adjustments are critical for this scene:

- **Particle-level collision** is enabled to achieve precise interaction with thin car body panels.
- **Collision detection distance** is increased above the default of 1. Without this, particles struggle to stick to the underside of geometry. Increasing the detection distance allows water to convincingly adhere to overhanging surfaces and collect at lips.

### Index of Refraction Fix for Thin Water Sheets

A rendering artifact occurs when thin water sheets sit on the car surface: small air gaps between the water and the metal cause total internal reflection. Light rays entering the water hit the water-air interface at a shallow angle and reflect back inside the water instead of passing through to the car surface. This causes unrealistic bright reflections where the water samples the HDR environment instead of the car paint beneath.

The fix uses a distance-based IOR attribute:

- Compute the distance from each mesh point to the car collider surface.
- Points very close to the car (purple in visualization) get IOR set to 1.0 (no refraction -- light passes straight through).
- Points farther from the car (red in visualization) keep the normal water IOR of 1.33.
- In the shader, the IOR attribute is remapped from 0-1 to 0-1.33 and fed into the refraction input.

### Mist Burst Layer

A separate branch models mist bursts at each raindrop impact location. These are small, fast-moving particles simulated with a POP solver (not MPM), rendered as very small droplets to add high-frequency detail to the splash impacts.

### Condensation Layer

A non-MPM detail layer simulates condensation droplets on the car surface:

1. Many small points are scattered across the car surface with assigned pscale values.
2. A solver tracks whether MPM water is flowing over each condensation point.
3. When water flows over a point, its pscale is reduced to near zero (condensation is "wiped away").
4. Over time without water flow, the pscale gradually restores (condensation reforms).
5. A condensation attribute controls the effect, visualized as red (full pscale) to purple (reduced).

### Dynamic Puddle with Ripple Simulation

Water particles that exit the simulation domain in front of the car drive a dynamic puddle effect:

1. A grid section is extracted in front of the car.
2. Points about to be deleted at the domain boundary are projected onto the puddle grid.
3. These points displace the grid surface.
4. A ripple solver creates wave propagation from the displacement points.
5. The final amplitude is scaled to 25% to keep the effect subtle.

Static puddles are also placed around the car for environmental context.

### Meshing the MPM Simulation

The MPM Surface node uses VDB from Particles with sequential filtering: dilation, erosion, then smoothing. This sequence produces a reasonable liquid look. The Neural Point Surface with liquid model is mentioned as a potential alternative but was not used in this scene.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Source the splash crown meshes | Continuous emission enabled |
| MPM Configure | Water material setup | Preset: water (default settings) |
| MPM Solver | Simulate water splashes | Surface tension: strong; min substeps: increased; material condition: reduced; substeps doubled |
| MPM Collider | Car body collision | Particle-level collision: enabled; detection distance: increased above default of 1 |
| MPM Surface | Mesh the water simulation | VDB from Particles; dilation, erosion, smoothing applied in sequence |
| VDB from Particles | Build splash crown shapes | Used in splash modeling branch |
| POP Solver | Mist burst simulation | Separate from MPM, renders as tiny droplets |
| Ripple Solver | Dynamic puddle waves | Amplitude scaled to 25% |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Prepare the car model** -- Add thickness to windows for refraction. Generate a watertight version for collision.
2. **Define raindrop impact locations** -- Scatter points on a grid above the car, project onto the car surface. Build oriented frames using surface normals with random rotation.
3. **Model the splash crowns** -- Copy a circle to each impact point. Procedurally shape the splash crown geometry. Convert to VDB, transfer velocity back to the mesh for MPM sourcing.
4. **Create synchronized rain** -- Use the reverse-time technique: start from impact positions, simulate backward to emission origins, then flip time and velocity. Instance spheres on the raindrop points for rendering.
5. **Configure the MPM simulation** -- Use the water preset with strong surface tension. Increase minimum substeps for stability. Reduce material condition. Double substeps. Enable particle-level collision and increase detection distance.
6. **Kill exiting particles** -- Delete points that hit the ground to conserve memory.
7. **Build the mist layer** -- Model mist burst shapes at impact locations. Simulate with a POP solver for fast, small particles.
8. **Mesh the water** -- Use MPM Surface with VDB from Particles. Apply dilation, erosion, and smoothing in sequence.
9. **Fix IOR for thin water sheets** -- Compute distance to car surface. Set IOR to 1.0 for points close to the car, 1.33 for points farther away. Remap in the shader from 0-1 to 0-1.33.
10. **Add condensation** -- Scatter points on car. Use a solver to reduce pscale when MPM water flows over them and restore pscale over time.
11. **Create the ground and puddles** -- Build a ground plane with static puddles. Add a dynamic puddle in front of the car driven by deleted simulation particles, with a ripple solver at 25% amplitude.

## Tips & Insights

- Simulate only the splashes with MPM, not the falling raindrops. Instance spheres on the rain points and render them separately to save significant memory.
- The reverse-time rain trick ensures perfect synchronization between raindrop impacts and splash emission without complex timing logic.
- Increase collision detection distance above the default of 1 when you need water to stick to the underside of geometry or collect at surface lips. This is essential for realistic water behavior on complex surfaces.
- Enable particle-level collision for precise interaction with thin geometry like car body panels.
- Watch for total internal reflection artifacts when rendering thin water sheets on surfaces. Use a distance-based IOR attribute (1.0 near the surface, 1.33 farther away) to eliminate the problem in the shader.
- Strong surface tension requires more substeps for stability. Increase minimum substeps and reduce the material condition number to compensate.
- Kill particles at domain boundaries to manage memory, especially in scenes with continuous emission.
- The dynamic puddle recommendation: extend it along the sides of the car (not just the front) for better integration of water being deleted at domain edges.
- The Neural Point Surface with liquid model is a viable alternative to VDB from Particles for meshing water simulations.

# MPM Wolf Snow

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JUcON39F7zE)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates a character-interaction snow simulation where three wolves run through a snow-covered terrain, kicking up particles and leaving trails. The setup showcases several advanced optimization techniques: camera frustum culling to limit the simulation domain, depth-based volume tapering to reduce point counts beneath the surface, and the MPM sleeping mechanism to deactivate passive particles. The tutorial also covers terrain preparation, static/dynamic snow splitting, secondary debris emission, volume rendering with SDF masking to preserve snow structure, and environmental dressing with snow-covered trees.

## Key Concepts

### Wolf Asset Preparation

The wolf animation (sourced from the SideFX content library) is prepared through several stages:

- **Animation smoothing** -- The raw animation is smoothed before further processing.
- **Fur simulation** -- A Vellum simulation is run on the wolf's fur guides, then cached.
- **Duplication** -- The single wolf is duplicated to create three wolves running through the scene.
- **Multiple output versions** -- The wolf geometry is prepared in different forms: a collider version (body + fur rasterized as VDB), a render version (with computed velocity for motion blur), and the fur itself for final Karma rendering.

### Camera Frustum Culling for Simulation Domain

A significant optimization technique clips the simulation domain to only what the camera sees:

1. Trail the wolves' paths over the first ~100 frames to establish their trajectories.
2. Compare the trajectories against the render camera's frustum.
3. Clip the snow volume to only the region visible to the camera (with padding before and after the visible range).
4. Convert the clipped region to VDB for use as the simulation domain boundary.

This avoids simulating snow in areas that will never appear on screen.

### Terrain and Snow Volume Construction

The snow terrain is built procedurally:

1. Generate a bounding box around the wolf trajectories.
2. Set the snow thickness.
3. Add surface detail (noise patterns simulating wind-sculpted snow patches).
4. Convert to SDF.
5. Cut out the camera-visible simulation region.

### Depth-Based Volume Tapering

An optimization reduces the simulated volume beneath the snow surface:

1. Observe how deep the wolf paws penetrate the snow.
2. Project the snow volume's bottom surface toward the wolves.
3. At greater depth, pull the volume boundary closer to where the paws actually reach.
4. Near the surface, lerp back to the original snow volume boundary.

This reduces the total simulation volume while keeping sufficient depth where the wolves interact with the snow, allowing higher resolution where it matters.

### Static vs. Dynamic Snow Splitting

The snow is split into two categories:

- **Dynamic snow** -- The region around the wolf paths, filled with MPM points that will be actively simulated. This is the carved-out region after frustum culling and depth tapering.
- **Static snow** -- Everything else visible to the camera, rendered as a static collider. A hole is cut in the static snow where the dynamic region exists.

To ensure seamless blending at render time, fine surface detail (bumpiness) is added to the static snow mesh to match the granular texture that MPM points produce when rasterized to a density grid.

An extension mesh covers any remaining areas visible to the camera that neither the dynamic nor the initial static snow covers.

### Collider Configuration

Two collider types are used with different friction/stickiness settings:

- **Wolf collider (deforming)** -- Body + rasterized fur VDB. Low stickiness so snow does not adhere excessively to the paws.
- **Static snow collider** -- High stickiness, simulating wet snow bonding to other wet snow, as expected in nature.

### Snow Material and Stiffness Noise

The dynamic snow uses the snow preset with modifications:

- Stiffness is multiplied up slightly to produce larger cohesive chunks.
- Noise is applied to stiffness values to add variation. The noise is remapped to a range of 5 to 2, then multiplied against the base stiffness. Any noise pattern works; the key is introducing spatial variation.

### Sleeping Mechanism for Performance

The sleeping (deactivation) system is critical for this mostly-passive simulation:

- The velocity threshold for deactivation is increased to make the solver more aggressive about putting particles to sleep.
- Particles far from the wolves' influence quickly become passive, saving significant computation.
- The simulation state can be visualized: purple = passive/sleeping, pink = active, with boundary particles also visible.
- A detail attribute string provides real-time statistics (e.g., "50% active, 44% passive, 5% boundary"). This can be linked to a Font SOP for on-screen stats during flipbooks.
- By the end of the simulation, up to 98% of particles may be passive at any given frame.

### Meshing Snow to SDF

The simulated MPM snow is converted to an SDF using VDB from Particles with conservative filtering:

- Dilation and erosion are kept small to preserve the granular look rather than creating sticky-looking clumps.
- Smoothing is applied to create a distribution of detail frequencies: smooth patches, mid-frequency shapes, and high-frequency small bits of snow.
- The goal is a natural mix of low, mid, and high frequency surface detail.

### Volume Rendering with SDF Masking

For rendering snow as a density volume, the "mask by surface" toggle on MPM Surface is essential:

- Without masking: The rasterized density looks uniformly fuzzy and grainy, lacking structural definition.
- With masking: The SDF representation is used as a mask on the density grid, preserving the overall snow structure while retaining fine particle detail.

This produces volumes with clear structural shapes plus granular surface texture, which is the desired look for snow.

### Secondary Debris

The MPM Debris node generates source points for a secondary POP simulation:

- JP attribute (stretching) multiplier increased to 5x to reduce emission from stretched areas.
- Slow-moving particle emission multiplier increased to 2x to reduce that source as well.
- Point replication reduced from 5 to 3 in both dimensions.
- Everything else at default.

The secondary simulation uses the same POP network pattern as other shots in the series. The debris is also rasterized to a density grid using MPM Surface, with the voxel size matched to the main simulation. The density multiplier for the secondary particles is typically dialed in during rendering in LOPs/Karma rather than in SOPs.

### Environmental Dressing

Trees are instanced on both sides of the wolf paths with snow added to branches. This is optional environmental detail handled in the LOP network and TOP network. The TOP network has significant baking requirements for the tree snow, which can be skipped if not needed.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Fill the dynamic snow volume with points | Snow preset |
| MPM Configure | Set snow material properties | Preset: snow; stiffness: multiplied up; stiffness noise: remapped 5-2 range |
| MPM Solver | Simulate snow interaction | Sleeping: enabled; velocity threshold: increased for aggressive deactivation |
| MPM Collider (wolves) | Deforming wolf body + fur collider | Low stickiness/friction |
| MPM Collider (static snow) | Static terrain collider | High stickiness (wet snow behavior) |
| MPM Surface | Mesh/rasterize snow points | VDB from Particles; small dilation/erosion; mask by surface: enabled |
| MPM Debris | Generate secondary particle sources | JP multiplier: 5x; slow particle multiplier: 2x; point replication: 3 (both axes) |
| Vellum Solver | Fur simulation on wolf guides | Pre-cached |
| Trail SOP | Track wolf trajectories | ~100 frames baked |
| VDB from Particles | Convert terrain to SDF | Used in terrain construction |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Prepare the wolf asset** -- Smooth the animation. Run a Vellum fur simulation and cache it. Duplicate the wolf to create three instances. Generate collider, render, and fur versions.
2. **Trail the wolf paths** -- Compute trajectories over the first ~100 frames to understand where the wolves travel through the scene.
3. **Clip to camera frustum** -- Use the render camera to identify the visible region. Clip the wolf paths and snow volume to this region with padding. Convert to VDB.
4. **Build the terrain** -- Generate a bounding box around the wolves. Set snow thickness and add wind-sculpted surface detail noise. Convert to SDF.
5. **Taper the volume by depth** -- Project the bottom surface toward the wolves at depth, lerp back to original near the surface. This reduces simulation volume while maintaining depth where paws interact.
6. **Split static and dynamic snow** -- The carved region becomes dynamic MPM snow. Everything else becomes a static collider with a hole cut for the dynamic region. Add surface bumpiness to the static mesh for blending.
7. **Add camera-fill extensions** -- Create additional static snow geometry to cover any remaining camera-visible areas.
8. **Configure colliders** -- Set wolves to deforming collider with low stickiness. Set static snow to high stickiness for wet-snow behavior.
9. **Configure the snow material** -- Use the snow preset. Multiply stiffness slightly. Apply noise (remapped 5-2) to stiffness for spatial variation.
10. **Enable sleeping** -- Activate the sleeping mechanism with an increased velocity threshold for aggressive deactivation of passive particles.
11. **Simulate** -- Run the MPM simulation. Monitor the state attribute for active/passive/boundary particle ratios.
12. **Mesh the snow** -- Convert to SDF using VDB from Particles with small dilation/erosion. Enable "mask by surface" for volume rendering to preserve snow structure.
13. **Generate and simulate debris** -- Use MPM Debris with increased JP and slow-particle multipliers, reduced point replication. Run through the standard POP debris network.
14. **Rasterize debris to density** -- Use MPM Surface matching the main simulation voxel size. Merge with the main snow volume. Adjust density multiplier at render time in LOPs.
15. **Dress the environment** -- Optionally instance snow-covered trees along the wolf paths via LOP and TOP networks.

## Tips & Insights

- Camera frustum culling is one of the most impactful optimizations for character-interaction snow scenes. Only simulate what the camera actually sees.
- Depth-based volume tapering further reduces simulation cost by narrowing the snow volume at depth where the wolves' paws do not reach, while keeping full volume near the surface.
- The sleeping mechanism can reduce active particle counts to as low as 2% of total particles in mostly-passive scenes. Increase the velocity threshold to make deactivation more aggressive.
- The detail attribute string on the simulation output provides real-time active/passive/boundary particle statistics. Link it to a Font SOP for visual monitoring during flipbooks.
- When meshing snow, keep dilation and erosion small to preserve the granular look. The goal is a natural mix of low, mid, and high frequency surface detail.
- Always enable "mask by surface" when rendering snow as density volumes. Without it, the rasterized density looks uniformly fuzzy and loses structural definition.
- Match static snow surface detail to the granularity of the rasterized dynamic snow points to ensure seamless blending at render time.
- Stiffness noise (any noise pattern, remapped to a useful range and multiplied against base stiffness) adds natural variation to how snow chunks break apart.
- For static colliders representing existing snow, use high stickiness to simulate wet snow bonding. For character colliders, use low stickiness so snow does not excessively adhere.
- Particles exiting the camera frustum can be killed to further optimize the simulation -- this is left as an exercise but is straightforward to implement.
- Density multiplier for secondary debris is best adjusted during rendering in LOPs/Karma, not in the SOP-level setup.

# MPM Pumpkin Smash

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OVQAAlh-3s8)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates a multi-layered organic destruction setup where a pumpkin is smashed by an animated hammer in slow motion. The pumpkin is split into three distinct material layers -- outer skin, fibrous flesh, and seeds -- each with its own MPM material configuration. The tutorial covers the full production pipeline: material layering and point optimization, slow-motion time scaling with correct velocity handling, secondary debris emission, meshing with UV transfer and smoothing masks, and rendering the seed pieces using MPM Deform Pieces. This is one of the more involved example scenes, showcasing how to combine multiple material types and post-simulation nodes into a compact, production-ready setup.

## Key Concepts

### Multi-Layer Material Setup

The pumpkin is decomposed into three separate components, each modeled and configured independently:

- **Outer Skin** -- A thin shell with some thickness. Uses a material derived from the snow preset with compression hardening enabled. Provides the structural exterior that fractures on impact.
- **Flesh** -- Fibrous interior geometry with fibers oriented from the outer skin toward the core. This fiber orientation influences both the simulation behavior (how the material tears) and the render appearance. The material starts from the snow preset with zero compression hardening, then is iterated to achieve the desired look.
- **Seeds** -- Small seed models scattered and oriented toward the pumpkin center. These use a rubber-like preset and are simulated as rigid pieces that get deformed/moved by the MPM solver.

There is no single "correct" recipe for these materials. The approach is to start from a preset (snow or rubber), then iterate until the simulation produces the desired visual result.

### Point Optimization and Attribute Transfer

A key optimization technique is demonstrated: instead of using the points directly output by MPM Source, the flesh model's points are kept and fused to eliminate overlaps (reducing from 40 million to 9 million points). The MPM material attributes are then configured separately and transferred onto these optimized points. This proves that you do not need to simulate the exact points coming out of the MPM Source node -- you can configure materials on one set of points and transfer the attributes to another.

After merging all components (skin, flesh, seeds), another overlap-deletion pass reduces the total from 14 million to 12 million points. Finally, stiffness is globally increased across all materials based on simulation iteration.

### Slow-Motion Time Scaling

The simulation runs in slow motion using a time scale parameter on the MPM Solver. Several velocity adjustments are required to handle this correctly:

- **For rendering:** Velocity vectors must be multiplied by the time scale so they represent actual per-frame motion in the slowed-down timeline.
- **For debris emission:** Velocity vectors must be divided by the time scale to recover real-time velocities, because the secondary debris simulation needs proper physical velocities for correct behavior.
- The MPM Debris node automatically imports the time scale from the simulation branch, so features like "spread points along velocity" correctly account for slow motion without manual adjustment.

### Simulation Start Frame and Clamping

The simulation starts at frame 32 (when the hammer impact occurs). A "clamp to first frame" node ensures the pumpkin geometry is visible from frame 1 onward, even though no simulation runs until frame 32.

### Secondary Debris

The MPM Debris node generates source points for a secondary POP simulation. Configuration adjustments include:

- Increased minimum speed threshold to exclude slow-moving points from emission.
- Reduced point replication parameters to emit fewer particles.
- Only 10% of generated points are kept from the debris node output.
- Seeds are excluded from debris emission.

The secondary POP simulation includes air resistance (with packing-based attenuation so densely packed points resist drag more) and collision handling.

A separate secondary layer renders as tiny water droplets / spray for high-frequency detail. This layer also retains only 10% of points.

### Meshing with MPM Surface

The post-simulation meshing pipeline leverages MPM Surface and related nodes, which embed much of the previously manual technology into compact node trees.

**Skin Mesh:**
- A depth attribute is computed to vary the surface color between interior and exterior at render time (smooth transition between two colors).
- UVs are transferred from a rest model via the third input of MPM Surface.
- Surface parameters: no dilation, some smoothing, some erosion.
- Smoothing masks protect areas of interest: the JP attribute (tearing/stretching regions) and curvature-based masks both exclude high-detail areas from smoothing.

**Flesh Mesh:**
- Produces the fibrous look directly from the simulation.
- Adaptivity increased by a factor of 10 to reduce polygon count (target: fitting within GPU memory for Karma XPU). Even so, the mesh reaches approximately 28 million polygons.

**Seed Pieces:**
- Uses MPM Deform Pieces without the MPM Post Structure node.
- Each seed gets a name attribute, then MPM Deform Pieces moves the original seed models according to the simulated point motion.
- The deformed seeds retain UVs and other render attributes from the original models.
- Final output is baked to poly soup.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Generate simulation points from geometry | Particle separation (driven by MPM Container) |
| MPM Configure | Define material properties per layer | Preset: snow (skin/flesh), rubber (seeds); compression hardening: 0 (flesh), nonzero (skin); stiffness multiplied up globally |
| MPM Solver | Run the simulation | Material condition: 7; time scale (custom); domain wall deletion enabled |
| MPM Collider | Animated hammer collider | Default settings |
| MPM Surface | Mesh the simulated points | Dilation: off (skin); smoothing: on; erosion: on; mask smooth by JP attribute and curvature; adaptivity: 10x (flesh); VDB from particles mode |
| MPM Debris | Generate secondary particle sources | Minimum speed: increased; point replication: reduced; keep ratio: 10% |
| MPM Deform Pieces | Move seed models with sim data | Name attribute required on each piece |
| Clamp to First Frame | Show geometry before sim start | Sim starts at frame 32 |
| POP Solver | Secondary debris simulation | Air resistance with packing; collision handling |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Model the pumpkin layers** -- Split the pumpkin into skin (outer shell with thickness), flesh (fibrous interior oriented toward core), and seeds (small models scattered and oriented toward center).
2. **Optimize point counts** -- Keep geometry points, fuse overlapping points to reduce count significantly, then configure MPM materials separately and transfer attributes.
3. **Configure materials** -- Start from presets (snow for skin/flesh, rubber for seeds). Iterate on compression hardening, stiffness, and other parameters until the simulation looks right. Increase global stiffness as needed.
4. **Set up the collider** -- Animate the hammer in real time at the expected impact speed. Apply the simulation time scale to achieve slow motion.
5. **Configure the MPM Solver** -- Set material condition to 7 for more aggressive substepping. Enable domain wall deletion for escaping points. Set the time scale parameter.
6. **Handle simulation start frame** -- Use a clamp-to-first-frame node so the pumpkin is visible before the impact frame (frame 32).
7. **Adjust velocity for rendering** -- Multiply velocity vectors by the time scale so motion blur renders correctly in the slow-motion timeline.
8. **Generate debris sources** -- Use MPM Debris with increased minimum speed, reduced point replication, and 10% retention. Exclude seeds. Reverse the velocity time-scale adjustment so debris emits with real-time velocities.
9. **Simulate secondaries** -- Run a POP simulation with air resistance (packing-aware) and collisions. Add a second spray/droplet layer for high-frequency detail, also at 10% retention.
10. **Mesh the skin** -- Use MPM Surface with smoothing and erosion. Transfer UVs from rest model via third input. Compute depth attribute for render-time color variation. Enable smoothing masks on JP (tearing) and curvature to protect detail.
11. **Mesh the flesh** -- Use MPM Surface with VDB from Particles and 10x adaptivity to manage polygon count for GPU rendering.
12. **Deform the seeds** -- Assign name attributes to seeds, then use MPM Deform Pieces to move the original high-quality seed models. Bake to poly soup.

## Tips & Insights

- You do not need to use the points output by MPM Source directly. You can configure materials on a separate point set and transfer the attributes, which allows point-count optimization via fusing.
- Start from material presets and iterate. There is no single correct recipe for organic destruction -- tweak compression hardening, stiffness, and other parameters until you achieve the desired look.
- When working in slow motion, remember that velocity vectors need different scaling depending on context: multiply by time scale for rendering (motion blur), divide by time scale for secondary emission (physical accuracy).
- The MPM Debris node automatically imports time scale from the simulation, so "spread points along velocity" works correctly without manual adjustment.
- Use smoothing masks (JP attribute and curvature) on MPM Surface to protect high-detail areas like tears and sharp features from being smoothed away.
- Increase MPM Surface adaptivity to reduce polygon count when targeting GPU renderers like Karma XPU.
- For rigid pieces within an MPM simulation (like seeds), use MPM Deform Pieces to drive high-quality source models rather than meshing the simulated points directly.
- The post-simulation node tree in Houdini 21 is much more compact than in previous versions, with most meshing technology embedded directly in the MPM Surface and related nodes.
